Streets will offer their stories if I am quiet enough.
I carry nothing but a coat, a notebook, and time.
The first streetlamp flickers, then steadies, then trusts me tonight.

Every block remembers a version of me I almost lost.
The bakery where I bought bread on rainy mornings returns.
The cracked sidewalk maps the winters I refused to name.
A blue gate leans as if tired of holding secrets.
I touch the brick wall and feel the day warming.
Once I lived nearby, young and certain of small things.
I thought happiness was a place I could find later.
Now I know it often passes disguised as ordinary weather.
A bus sighs at the corner, exhaling light and people.
I watch them scatter like seeds across the waking street.

The first cafe lifts its shade and lets morning out.
A woman wipes tables while her child draws on paper.
The smell of coffee enters the street like a hand.
I order a cup and stand near the window listening.
Two old men argue about a game nobody remembers clearly.
Their voices are soft, worn smooth by years of friendship.
Outside, a delivery truck unloads crates of bright fruit.

I drink slowly, grateful for warmth against my cold palms.

Gulls wheel above it, shouting like small angry prophets.

Above, wires stitch the sky into a careful grid.

They hold what we drop and keep what we forget.

Maybe that is enough for anyone learning to live.

Enough to witness and be witnessed in return.
Enough to carry a small poem against your chest while the world continues turning without apology tonight too.

The poem in my pocket has become a companion.
I imagine its underlined line traveling into my blood.
Rain may come again, but I am less afraid.

A timetable glows blue above the waiting benches.

We do not speak, yet we share the same uncertainty.
Every platform is a border between one self and another.

I think of all the goodbyes they have carried.
I think of the reunions that followed like weather.
Departure is not always abandonment; sometimes it is practice for learning how to remain human together still.

I board and choose a seat facing backward.
I like watching where I have been for once.

Then the river, black and patient, reflecting nothing.
Then the dark fields where the city loses confidence.

A man writes in a notebook with urgent calm.
I close my eyes and let motion think for me while the night carries me gently homeward through quiet miles of sleep.

Perhaps it will demand patience, courage, or apology.
Perhaps it will offer only small tasks and weather.
Either way, I will carry this walk inside me.
The city gave me its lights, its rain, its silence.
It reminded me that attention is a form of love.
To notice is to participate in the world honestly.
To walk is to believe that direction still matters.
To write this down is to say it mattered.
Somewhere ahead, morning is already preparing its first blue line and the world begins again with us.
